newsitem.title: ROMANIA: HUNGARY PRESIDENT IN ROMANIA ON "HISTORIC" VISIT.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY PRESIDENT IN ROMANIA ON "HISTORIC" VISIT.

text.p: The presidents of Romania and Hungary, once uneasy neighbours, met on Sunday and said warming relations could help both countries join NATO and the European Union.
Hungary's Arpad Goncz arrived in Bucharest on Sunday for a three-day visit which he hailed as "historic", the first by a Hungarian head of state for 70 years.
"Our talks have been very sincere...our positions were identical," Hungarian President Arpad Goncz told reporters after meeting his Romanian counterpart Emil Constantinescu.
"The intentions are clear...our intention is to boost political relations at all levels."

During his visit Goncz will meet senior officials and representatives of Romania's 1.6 million ethnic Hungarians. He will visit the Transylvanian cities of Tirgu Mures and Cluj, where he is likely to discuss the opening of a Hungarian consulate.

Ties between Romania and Hungary have been tainted until recently by what Hungary saw as Romania's poor treatment of its Hungarian minority and by Romanian suspicion that Hungary has territorial designs on Transylvania.
Last September, the two countries signed a political treaty which put an end to political sabre-rattling and laid the grounds for reconciliation.
Romania's new centrist government, which ousted the former leftist cabinet in elections last November, has launched a fast-paced crusade to implement the treaty.

Last week, the government amended the education and local administration laws, giving minorities the right of tuition in their mother tongue at all levels as well as the right to use their language in court or administration.
"We are freed from all problems which led to hatred and disagreements in the past. We can deal now with real problems and a real democracy, not an abstarct one," Constantinescu told journalists.
Good relations between Romania and Hungary are seen by Western democracies as vital for both countries' ambitions to join the EU and NATO.
"Our countries have identical interests as far as Euro-Atlantic integration is concerned," Goncz said, adding that Hungary would support Romania's NATO bid.
Romania hopes to be invited to join along with favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic, when NATO announces its first eastward expansion at a Madrid summit in July. REUTER 251333 GMT may 97
